issues.legal_issue: Quashing an acquisition at the instance of some landowners does not, without more, nullify the acquisition of land belonging to owners who did not challenge it.
material_facts: The acquisition covered a large area, and only some landowners challenged it.

The relief sought by the owner whose case was later relied on was limited to quashing the declaration as it related to his own land; he did not seek quashing of the preliminary notification or the entire acquisition.
The landowners seeking reconveyance had not challenged the acquisition, and the record did not establish that the earlier court orders had quashed the acquisition in its entirety.
A substantial portion of the acquired land had already been used for housing and other purposes.
issues.conclusion: The earlier order quashing the acquisition for a particular landowner did not nullify the acquisition of the land belonging to the other landowners.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on Shyamnandan Prasad v. State of Bihar (1999) 4 SCC 255, Abhey Ram v. Union of India (1997) 5 SCC 421, and Delhi Administration v. Gurdip Singh Uban (1999) 7 SCC 44 and (2000) 7 SCC 296 for the principle that quashing acquisition proceedings at the instance of one or a few landowners does not nullify the entire acquisition. The scope of relief is also confined by the challenge and relief actually sought.

predicates.acquisition_challenged_by_some_owners: Some owners challenged the acquisition of land that formed part of a larger acquisition.
predicates.relief_limited_to_challengers_land: The challenger sought relief limited to the land belonging to that challenger.
predicates.other_owners_did_not_challenge: The owners whose land is in dispute did not challenge the acquisition.
predicates.whole_acquisition_quashing_not_establish: The record did not establish that a court had quashed the acquisition as a whole.

issues.definition: When some owners challenge an acquisition and the challenge or established relief is limited, the acquisition remains effective for the land of owners who did not challenge it.

issues.legal_issue: The power to reconvey acquired land is limited to land that remains vested in the government and is no longer required for the acquisition purpose or any other public purpose, and reconveyance cannot be compelled when those conditions are not met.
material_facts: After compensation was paid, the acquired land was transferred to the housing board.
The board had used a substantial portion of the acquired land for housing, roads, residential plots, a school, and other purposes.
The board reported that the housing scheme remained in progress and that portions of the disputed land were allocated or intended for public uses.
The government rejected the owners’ requests for reconveyance after considering the board’s report.
issues.conclusion: The government could not reconvey land that had already been transferred to the housing board, and the owners could not compel reconveyance where the land remained usable for a public purpose.
issues.legal_principle: Section 48-B of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, as applicable in the State, permits the government to transfer acquired land to the original owner only when the land remains vested in the government and the government is satisfied that it is not required for the purpose of acquisition or any other public purpose; the owner must be willing to repay the compensation and applicable statutory amounts. The provision is an exception to the general rule and must be strictly construed. The housing board, as the receiving agency, was not competent to transfer the land under that provision. The Court also referred to Tamil Nadu Housing Board v. Keeravani Ammal and State of Kerala v. M. Bhaskaran Pillai (1997) 5 SCC 432.

predicates.reconveyance_request_after_acquisition: An original owner sought reconveyance of land after it had been acquired and compensation had been paid.
predicates.land_transferred_to_another_agency: The government had transferred the acquired land to another agency.
predicates.public_purpose_remains_available: The land continued to be used, or remained available for use, for a public purpose.

issues.definition: When an original owner seeks reconveyance after acquisition, transfer of the land to another agency or its continued availability for a public purpose means that the owner cannot compel reconveyance.

issues.legal_issue: A court exercising judicial review cannot set aside a government decision refusing reconveyance when the decision is supported by material showing an ongoing public purpose and no basis for finding the decision-making process unlawful has been established.
material_facts: The government rejected the reconveyance request after receiving a report that the land was proposed for housing and other public uses.
The housing scheme was still being implemented, and parts of the acquired land had been developed or allocated.
The owners had not pleaded or produced material showing bad faith, reliance on extraneous or irrelevant factors, or breach of natural justice.
The appellate court directed reconveyance without examining the government’s reasons or the factual record.
issues.conclusion: The appellate court could not use judicial review to annul the government’s refusal of reconveyance on the material presented.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 226 of the Constitution, a decision on reconveyance is not to be displaced merely because land is vacant or a claimant seeks its return. Judicial interference requires a demonstrated legal defect, such as arbitrariness, bad faith, reliance on extraneous or irrelevant considerations, or violation of natural justice. The Court applied the limits on judicial review stated by the Single Judge and referred to Tamil Nadu Housing Board v. Keeravani Ammal in rejecting an unsupported assumption that a scheme had been abandoned.

predicates.judicial_review_of_reconveyance_refusal: A court was asked to review a government decision refusing to reconvey acquired land.
predicates.public_purpose_supported_by_material: Material before the decision-maker supported the conclusion that the land remained needed or usable for a public purpose.
predicates.no_proven_decision_making_defect: The claimant did not establish bad faith, reliance on an extraneous or irrelevant factor, or breach of natural justice.

issues.definition: When a reconveyance refusal is reviewed, material supporting a continuing public purpose and the absence of a proven decision-making defect mean that the court cannot set the refusal aside.

issues.legal_issue: Previous releases of acquired land do not establish discriminatory treatment when the record does not show that the other cases were substantially similar.
material_facts: Some portions of the acquired land had been released to other owners pursuant to court orders.
The owners did not provide the pleadings and other materials from those cases needed to assess whether the claims were substantially similar.
The available material showed prior release orders but did not establish that the circumstances of those owners matched the circumstances of the owners seeking reconveyance.
issues.conclusion: The Court could not infer that the refusal to reconvey the disputed land was arbitrary or discriminatory based on the prior releases alone.
issues.legal_principle: A claim of unequal treatment requires a basis to compare the relevant circumstances; without materials establishing substantial similarity, prior relief to other owners does not establish a violation of Article 14 of the Constitution.

predicates.reconveyance_review_claiming_unequal_tre: A claimant challenged a refusal of reconveyance on the basis that other owners had received relief.
predicates.prior_releases_exist: Other owners had obtained releases of some acquired land.
predicates.comparable_case_material_missing: The claimant did not provide sufficient material to establish that the other owners’ cases were substantially similar.

issues.definition: In a reconveyance review alleging unequal treatment, prior releases do not establish discrimination when the material needed to show comparable cases is missing.

issues.legal_issue: Summary dismissals of special leave petitions do not lay down a legal rule binding in later cases.
material_facts: The owners relied on earlier High Court orders directing release of land and on special leave petitions dismissed by brief, unreasoned orders.
The Court found that the special leave petitions had been summarily dismissed, while one petition had been dismissed as withdrawn.
issues.conclusion: The earlier summary dismissal orders could not be treated as laying down law that later benches were required to follow.
issues.legal_principle: A summary dismissal of a special leave petition, without a reasoned determination of law, does not establish a legal precedent binding on coordinate or smaller benches.

predicates.precedential_effect_of_prior_special_lea: A court was asked to treat earlier special leave petition orders as governing a later case.
predicates.prior_petitions_dismissed_summarily: The earlier petitions were dismissed without reasoned judgments determining a legal issue.

issues.definition: When a court considers the precedential effect of earlier special leave orders, summary dismissals do not supply a binding legal rule.
